segments.text: Rosa lleva el libro grande de la biblioteca a la mesa pequeña del patio. Ana deja su mapa cerca del cuaderno de Elena. El papel viejo tiene «Elena. Sala del patio». No hay lluvia en nuestro patio. En la sala, el techo está mojado encima del estante; hay una gota en la pared. Elena lleva su cuaderno lejos de la ventana cerrada. Elena lee su nombre. Luis presta su libro rojo a Ana. Ana abre el libro y busca otro cuento.

En la página hay un dibujo: un gato está fuera de una casa. La puerta está cerrada. Debajo del dibujo está «La casa». Ana lee en voz alta: «El gato está en la calle. Una persona abre la puerta de su casa. La persona entra; el gato no entra. El gato espera fuera. La puerta está cerrada».

grammar.title: Gramática
grammar.rule: Me gusta el cuento; me gustan los dibujos. A Ana y a Rosa les gusta la fruta.

tables.caption: por qué · porque
rows: Porque el gato no entra en la casa.

grammar.note_en:
Gustar expresses liking, but its Spanish structure differs from English “like”. In Me gusta el cuento, the tale is the grammatical subject: it is the thing that is pleasing. Me identifies the person who likes it: the speaker. Translate this naturally as “I like the tale”. Do not copy the English order into a Spanish subject-and-verb pattern. Me gusta la música means “I like music”; Me gustan los dibujos means “I like the drawings”. Gusta agrees with a singular subject such as música, cuento or pan; gustan agrees with a plural subject such as dibujos. The number of people doing the liking does not decide between gusta and gustan.

The person forms in this chapter are me, “to me”; te, “to you” for one familiar listener; le, “to him/her” or respectful singular “to you”; nos, “to us”; les, “to them” or plural “to you”. They stand before gusta/gustan. No precedes the whole group: No me gusta el cuento means “I do not like the tale”. ¿Te gustan los dibujos? means “Do you like the drawings?” A question still agrees with the drawings, not with the listener. A named phrase can make the person explicit: A Luis le gustan los dibujos means “Luis likes the drawings”; A Ana y a Rosa les gusta la fruta means “Ana and Rosa like fruit”. In the latter, two people like one substance, so les is plural but gusta singular. Do not omit the le or les in this model just because the names are already present.

The reference table translates as follows: me gusta el cuento / me gustan los dibujos, “I like the tale / the drawings”; te gusta el cuento / te gustan los dibujos, “you like the tale / the drawings”; le gusta la canción / le gustan los dibujos, “he or she likes the song / the drawings”, with Luis explicitly named in the scene; nos gusta el pan / nos gustan los dibujos, “we like the bread / the drawings”; les gusta la fruta / les gustan los dibujos, “they like the fruit / the drawings”, with the named groups establishing the people. The complete Spanish sentences around each example show whose preference is expressed. The words le/les do not identify a person’s gender. Context also distinguishes third-person reference from direct respectful address, as in ¿Les gusta el pan?, “Do you like the bread?”, addressing Ana and Luis.

Preferir names a preference between possibilities. Prefiero otra historia means “I prefer another story”; ¿Prefieres el cuento de tu libro? means “Do you prefer the tale in your book?”; Rosa prefiere su cuento means “Rosa prefers her tale”; prefieren escuchar su voz means “they prefer to listen to her voice”. The demonstrated singular forms have ie in the stem: prefiero, prefieres, prefiere. This chapter uses the shown prefieren with the group as well. A preference is a choice, not an inability: Rosa can read the tale and look at the illustrated page, but prefers a different ending. The large-print book also gives her independent access to the chosen story. These are separate reasons.

También adds a matching positive statement: A Ana le gusta la historia y a Elena también means “Ana likes the story, and Elena does too”. Tampoco adds a matching negative one: Tampoco me gusta el café amargo means “I do not like bitter coffee either”. Do not replace one with the other merely because both add another person. The negative meaning is already present in tampoco. A following no is not added in this chapter’s order; compare the equally negative sentence El cuento no me gusta tampoco, “I do not like the tale either”. The reading shows both placement patterns.

Por qué asks a reason: ¿Por qué no te gusta? means “Why do you not like it?” Porque introduces the answer: Porque el gato no entra en la casa means “Because the cat does not enter the house”. The question has two words and an accent on qué; the answer conjunction is one word without an accent. In Porque puedo leer las letras y porque me gusta la historia, “Because I can read the letters and because I like the story”, Rosa names both access and preference. The first why question in Pensum C follows those demonstrated reasons. Personal questions wait for a later chapter; the present C questions concern the story.

The printed canción is a song, with voice and music; the dibujo is a drawing and the foto a photograph. Pan is bread, café coffee, fruta fruit. Dulce means sweet and amargo bitter, describing the tastes of the particular drinks or foods here. The served items and tastes are fictional choices, not claims about every fruit or every coffee. The visitor’s identification of the person in the old photograph is a character claim. Rosa reports a different memory. The chapter does not establish the photographed person’s identity, the room’s former name or a resolution of the memory thread.
